title: Looking back: no excuse
hook: a discourse we passed: Sariputta tells a brahmin that duty to family does not excuse harming others

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ghatikara and his blind parents, and your line, the good potter. Did you do one task with honest hands? Today, another discourse we walked past, and a man who wasn't so honest. Day five hundred nineteen.

I'm doing it for my family. People say it about the best things they do, and sometimes about the worst. In the ninety-seventh discourse, Sariputta hears news about an old acquaintance, a brahmin named Dhananjani who works for the king. He's gotten careless, people say. He uses the king's authority to squeeze the brahmin householders, and uses the householders as cover to cheat the king. Sariputta goes to find him. Today, looking back: no excuse.
screen: `I'M DOING IT FOR MY FAMILY.` → `DHANANJANI, THE KING'S MAN.` → `SARIPUTTA GOES TO FIND HIM.`

segments.voice: Sariputta finds him at a cowshed while the cows are being milked. Dhananjani offers him fresh milk. Sariputta says he's already eaten for the day, and asks: Dhananjani, are you diligent? How can I be? the brahmin answers. I have my parents to support. A wife and children. Workers. Duties to friends, to ancestors, to the gods, to the king. And this body has to be fed too. It's an honest list, and a heavy one. Sariputta doesn't dismiss it. He asks a question instead. Suppose a man did harm, broke the moral law, for his parents' sake. And suppose that when he died, the wardens of the hell realms dragged him off. Could he say: I did it for my parents, let me go? Could his parents say: he did it for us, let him go? No, says Dhananjani. Then the same question, one by one. For wife and children? For workers? Friends? Ancestors? The gods? The king? For this body? No, every time. Sariputta asks one more. Who's better: the one who does wrong for his parents, or the one who does right for them? The one who does right. Then there are other ways, Sariputta says, ways in line with the dhamma, to earn a living, support your parents, and not do harm. The Pali word is dhammika: righteous, in keeping with the dhamma. The point isn't that family duty is bad. Elsewhere the discourses honor it. The point is that love for your own doesn't turn harm to others into something else. The duty stays. The excuse goes.
screen: `AT THE COWSHED, MILK OFFERED` · `I HAVE SO MANY TO SUPPORT` · `COULD HE SAY: I DID IT FOR THEM?` · `THERE ARE RIGHTEOUS WAYS` · then, large: `NO EXCUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one excuse you use. Sit quietly and let one come up. Maybe it's I'm too busy, or everyone does it, or it's for the kids. Hold it gently, the way Sariputta held Dhananjani's list. Is the duty real? Probably yes. Now ask: is there a way to meet it without the harm? Don't solve it all. Just see one other way. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. A second discourse we passed: duty to family is real, but it never makes harming others right. Today's word.
Your line: no excuse. Today, when you hear yourself say I had to, ask once whether there was a kinder way to do the same duty. Day five hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Buddhist ethics across schools honors support for parents and family as a duty while holding that right livelihood, earning without harming others, is part of the eightfold path; MN 97 is one place this is spelled out.

pairs: the brahmin who served the king
no excuse to the wardens of hell
righteous, in line with the dhamma

myth: Sariputta tells Dhananjani that supporting his family is a distraction
he never questions the duty; he questions the harm done in its name.
Sariputta turns down the milk because he disapproves of Dhananjani
he says only that he has already eaten for the day.
Dhananjani agrees that doing right for one's parents is better than doing wrong for them
and Sariputta says there are righteous ways to support them.

fork.setup: you're Sariputta. Dhananjani says: how can I be diligent? I have parents, wife, children, workers, king and gods to look after. what do you do?
options: ask whether harm done for their sake would be excused.
tell him to leave his family and become a monk.
agree that he has no choice.
fork.reveal: Sariputta asks question after question, and Dhananjani sees for himself: the duty is real, but no one can excuse the harm.

original.note: Pali dhammika: righteous, in keeping with the dhamma. the other way to support a family.

trapdoor: what you thought: if it's for your family, it's justified.
what it means: in MN 97 family duty is real, but it doesn't excuse harming others to meet it.

what a scholar hears: the discourse ends with Sariputta teaching the dying Dhananjani the way to the Brahma world, and the Buddha remarking that he could have taught him further: a gentle correction of Sariputta.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook's unsourced 'one of the oldest sentences there is' cut; myth about teaching by questions replaced (it repeated days 511-512) with the milk refusal; trapdoor's 'rare' correction and howItsDone's 'teachers often cite' removed.

MN 97 paraphrased. Confirm the report about Dhananjani (plundering the brahmins under the king's cover and the king under the brahmins' cover), the cowshed and milk scene, and the list of dependents (parents, wife and children, slaves and workers, friends, ancestors, deities, king, body).

Confirm the ending summarized in the trapdoor (Sariputta teaches the four brahmaviharas as the way to the Brahma world; the Buddha says he set him in an inferior Brahma world when more could be done).
The detail about Dhananjani's wives is omitted on purpose.
